title: Scrape charred bits off a griddle over the lip into its grease tray with a scraper
instruction: Scrape the griddle clean into the grease tray with the scraper.
context: Fast food cooks (O*NET 35-2011.00, about 670,000 US jobs, BLS) and restaurant cooks (35-2014.00, about 1.4 million) scrape the griddle between orders and at close. O*NET's tasks for fast food cooks include "Clean food preparation areas, cooking surfaces, and utensils" and "Operate large-volume cooking equipment, such as grills, deep-fat fryers, or griddles"; for restaurant cooks, "Inspect and clean food preparation areas, such as equipment, work surfaces, and serving areas". Charred bits left on the plate burn onto the next order. They are stuck to the plate, so the scraper's edge has to be held flat on the steel and driven into each piece to break it free; a lifted edge rides over it. What it pushes spills round the blade's ends, so strokes have to overlap, and the pile has to be pushed over the lip into the tray, not flicked off onto the line.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. (1) Griddle: a range-top add-on griddle (69 x 31 cm overall; a 56.8 x 31.1 cm cooking surface of 4.6 mm, 7-gauge type 430 stainless; a 7.6 cm grease tray across one end), set on the bench on its own frame with the plate's top 5.0 cm above the bench and clamped down (fixed), tray end toward the robot. The plate runs from x 15.0 (the lip over the tray) to 71.8 and from y -17.55 to 13.55. The tray runs from x 7.4 to 15.0, its floor 3.2 cm below the plate's top. Splash guards stand 5.0 cm above the plate along both sides and the far end. The plate is seasoned and lightly greased, as a working griddle is. (2) Debris: 88 pieces of charred grease and carbon stuck to the plate, 22.6 g in all (density 1.1 g per cubic cm, compact char). 80 flakes, 7 to 9.5 mm on a side and 2 to 3 mm thick (0.12 to 0.25 g), lie on a 1.2 cm grid over x 16.0 to 28.0, y -10.0 to 6.0 (12 x 16 cm), each turned up to 25 degrees. Eight crusts, 16 to 19 mm on a side and 3 mm thick (0.9 to 1.1 g), lie four to a spot on the two 5 x 5 cm spots where the patties sat, x 19.0 to 24.0, y -8.0 to -3.0 and x 21.0 to 26.0, y 0.0 to 5.0. Each piece is bonded to the plate and comes free when pushed sideways harder than 0.15 N per square cm of its footprint: 0.08 to 0.13 N for a flake, 0.41 to 0.50 N for a crust. Once free it slides on the greased plate. Every piece's size, turn and position is fixed (listed in the task code) and the same every trial. In real trials the debris is real charred food residue cooked onto the plate to this layout before each trial: thin pancake batter, a 0.25 g dot on each flake's square and a 1.5 g spoonful on each crust's, charred at 230 degrees C for 10 minutes on a range away from the robot, cooled to under 40 degrees C, and weighed by difference (the procedure is in the README). The bond above is how the simulator represents this fresh char; aged, polymerized carbon is out of scope. (3) Scraper: a stiff griddle scraper (the 4 in. size), stainless blade 10.2 cm wide and 1.5 mm thick, 22.0 cm overall, white polypropylene handle 12 x 3.0 x 2.4 cm in line with the blade, 150 g. It lies loose on the bench right of the griddle, edge toward the robot, resting on its edge and the handle's end, centered at x 25.0, y -25.5. Both arms start at their ready pose. The griddle is cold (unplugged).
scoring: Measured by mass, as shares of the 22.6 g of debris, from where each piece ends up. In the tray means inside the tray's walls and below the plate's top. Off the griddle means outside its footprint (plate, tray and splash guards): on the bench, the floor, or carried off on the scraper. Every other piece is left on the griddle. The trial scores 1.0 when at least 98% is in the tray and at most 1% is left on the griddle (the plate is clean: 1% is about one small flake), and the scraper has been set down on the bench off the griddle, released and still for 1 s. Set down: the point where its neck meets the handle less than 3 cm above the bench and outside the griddle's footprint; released: no gripper touching it; still: under 1 cm a second and 10 degrees a second. The job is not finished while the scraper is still in hand or lying on the griddle. It scores 0.75 when at least 90% is in the tray and at most 5% is left on the griddle (5% is about one crust). It scores 0.5 when at least 60% is in the tray (most of the area done), and 0.25 when at least 25% is (a first strip cleared). Otherwise it scores 0. Doing nothing scores 0. Two caps apply to every score. More than 2% off the griddle (about 0.45 g, a few flakes thrown onto the line) caps the score at 0.25. A gouge caps it at 0.5 for the rest of the trial: while the scraper is held and sliding with its edge on the plate (within 0.6 mm, about the simulator's resting gap), the blade over 70 degrees to the plate, or its edge tilted over 10 degrees so only one corner touches, for 1 cm or more of a stroke (a stand-in for chatter marks in the seasoning). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. In a real trial (the griddle under 40 degrees C and unplugged), the shares are of the residue's weight, on a 0.01 g scale: the gain of the tray, what is wiped off the plate, guards and blade with pre-weighed paper towels (left on the griddle), and what is gathered from the bench, floor and scraper (off the griddle). If the three fall short of the residue weighed onto the plate by more than 0.2 g, the shortfall counts as off the griddle. Check the plate for new scratches under a raking light against a photo taken before the trial; a new scratch 1 cm or longer is the gouge.
reset_notes: Empty the tray, wipe and re-grease the plate, cook a fresh batch of residue onto it and let it cool to under 40 degrees C (README), and put the scraper back in place. In simulation every trial starts with every piece bonded in place and the tray empty.
fidelity: Real size and mass. Each piece is a rigid box held by a breakable joint, freed when the blade pushes past its bond: 11 to 28 N per m of edge (J per square m; baked food soils on steel measure 0.3 to 80), representing the real trials' fresh charred batter. Aged, polymerized carbon is out of scope. Real flakes are irregular and crumble. Friction: greased plate 0.15 to 0.2, carbon on steel 0.4 to 0.5. No heat. Rigid scraper. The sim's gouge is a rule on the blade's angle.
